video_title: Why We Made Jev — Diogo Almeida, TypeSafe Co-founder & CEO
gist: Diogo Almeida (TypeSafe co-founder/CEO, ex-OpenAI) explains why TypeSafe built Jev, a new 'system one'/'machine native' model class designed for code (not chat) to be the consumer of AI output, arguing RLHF's mode-dropping and RLVR's benchmark-chasing are the wrong north stars for programmable, reliable software automation, and that TypeSafe's alternative training paradigm ('RLCD'), structured JSON API primitives, and anti-benchmark/anti-refusal philosophy are what let Jev go viral (>1 trillion tokens/day within a week) purely on developer word of mouth.

insights.claim: TypeSafe frames Jev as the first entrant in a new model class it calls 'system one' or 'machine native large programmable' models, explicitly designed so that code, not a human chatting, is the primary consumer of model output — distinct from pre-trained autocomplete LLMs, RLHF chat/instruction models, and RLVR reasoning models.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: Defines a distinct product category (models for software integration rather than chat) that investors should track separately from chatbot/reasoning-model competition when sizing TypeSafe's addressable market.
insights.quote: I think these are is the class of models where the goal is for code to be the consumer.

insights.claim: Jev is named for and explicitly optimized around 'intelligence per dollar,' referencing the Jevons paradox thesis that cheaper effective intelligence will increase, not decrease, total AI consumption and spend.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: Signals TypeSafe's core competitive axis is cost-efficiency of intelligence, not raw benchmark capability — a metric investors can watch as the company's stated differentiator versus frontier labs optimizing for absolute intelligence.

insights.claim: TypeSafe says it surpassed one trillion tokens processed per day within about a week of Jev's launch, and describes this usage as sustained 'even at night,' implying it is driven by machine/automated calls running in production rather than by curious one-off human chatbot queries.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: A trillion-tokens/day run rate within days of launch, sustained overnight, is a strong leading indicator of genuine production integration (not novelty traffic) — a concrete adoption metric to monitor for TypeSafe's growth trajectory.
insights.quote: A trillion tokens a day is a lot.

insights.claim: Almeida argues waitlist signups are a poor demand signal for developer platforms because many signers are non-developers who try a couple of queries and bounce; the real signal TypeSafe watches is developers hitting rate limits and requesting more capacity once they've extracted value.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: Investors evaluating developer-tool traction should discount headline signup/waitlist numbers and instead look for usage-expansion/rate-limit-upgrade requests as the true retention and value signal.
insights.quote: Signups to me don't really matter.

insights.claim: Almeida claims Jev occupies a largely 'unoccupied' quadrant of being both faster and cheaper than incumbent models while holding intelligence roughly constant, versus the industry-typical tradeoff of faster-but-more-expensive.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: If true and durable, this positions Jev as a genuine Pareto-frontier improvement rather than a mere cost play — a claim worth stress-testing against independent developer benchmarking over time.

insights.claim: TypeSafe explicitly plans to ship additional model 'shapes' beyond Jev, including possibly different-sized models with dynamic model selection, narrow fine-tuning for specific stacks, and other new machine-native primitive types beyond its current Nool/Score/Choice trio — positioning Jev as the opening move in a broader platform, not a one-off product.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: Signals a multi-product roadmap (an 'AWS of intelligence' ambition) rather than a single-SKU business, relevant to long-term TAM and platform-lock-in thesis for TypeSafe.

insights.claim: Almeida states that if TypeSafe disappeared entirely today, he estimates it would take the rest of the field roughly one to two years to catch up to what it has already unlocked, framing this as his own assessment of TypeSafe's current competitive moat durability.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: A founder's self-assessed moat window (1-2 years) is a useful anchor for investors modeling how long TypeSafe's first-mover advantage in machine-native models might last before commoditization.
insights.quote: if the whole company of type safe disappears like maybe it'll take like a year or two for people to like truly catch up

insights.claim: Almeida's central technical argument is that RLHF causes 'mode dropping' — collapsing away minority/rare valid outputs the way GANs drop minority classes to produce sharp images — versus 'mode covering' pre-GAN-style calibrated-but-blurry distributions; this mode-dropping is what makes RLHF'd chat models miscalibrated and brittle at generating long error-free strings.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: Gives investors a concrete mechanistic lens for why chat-tuned models hallucinate/overclaim confidence, and why TypeSafe bet its architecture on avoiding this failure mode for programmatic use.
insights.quote: This was like models before GANs. they made blurry images, right? Um, instead GANs mode drop.

insights.claim: Almeida argues Yann LeCun's well-known claim that autoregressive LLM error probability compounds catastrophically with sequence length is mathematically intuitive but empirically wrong for calibrated, mode-covering base models — and only becomes true once RLHF's mode-dropping forces the model into hyperconfident, brittle behavior.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: Offers a specific, falsifiable mechanistic rebuttal/refinement of a prominent AI-doom argument, useful for calibrating how seriously to weight LeCun-style 'LLMs are fundamentally limited' theses.
insights.quote: I actually think that among takes Yan Lun is among the most accurate.

insights.claim: Despite endorsing much of LeCun's critique, Almeida is skeptical or non-committal that LeCun's proposed fix (a JEPA-style joint-embedding/world-model approach) is currently practical, saying he prioritizes pragmatism over research elegance and declining to confirm it is deployable today.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: Suggests JEPA/world-model approaches remain pre-commercial per an informed insider, tempering near-term investment theses built around JEPA-style architectures displacing token-based LLMs.

insights.claim: Almeida frames LLM post-training history as having produced only about 2 to 2.2 genuinely new task 'north stars' to date: RLHF (optimizing for human-pleasing instruction-following) and RLVR (optimizing for verifiable/benchmark rewards) — with TypeSafe's unpublished 'RLCD' paradigm (optimizing for programmatic reliability) positioned as a third.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: If RLCD is a genuinely new, defensible training paradigm rather than a marketing label, it implies most RLVR-focused competitors are optimizing a well-mined vein while TypeSafe claims a differentiated, harder-to-replicate one.

insights.claim: Almeida calls the AI-safety 'pace of the frontier' pause debate a 'sleight of hand,' arguing it implicitly assumes labs must keep doing more open-ended RLVR (giving models latitude to 'do anything' to boost capability); TypeSafe rejects that premise entirely and does zero RLVR by design.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: Positions TypeSafe as structurally outside the RLVR capability race and its associated safety/pacing debate — relevant for assessing regulatory/reputational risk exposure differently than pure-RLVR reasoning-model labs.
insights.quote: I think zero is the optimal amount for our shape, right?

insights.claim: Almeida argues model refusal behavior is fundamentally 'a type error' in an API context because safety alignment (following the platform's/others' instructions) is architecturally opposed to capability alignment (following the developer's own instructions); conflating the two makes an API 'anti-developer,' so Jev's API is designed not to refuse, leaving policy enforcement to the developer's own decomposed logic.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: A structural bet that safety-by-refusal is the wrong design for API/infrastructure providers; investors should watch whether enterprise buyers accept a no-refusal API model or whether this becomes a liability/regulatory flashpoint as TypeSafe scales.
insights.quote: refusal is just like obviously a type error.

insights.claim: Almeida attributes widely-noted RLHF chat-model artifacts — sycophancy, overconfidence, hallucination, and stylistic tics like bolded/italicized text, emojis, and unnecessary follow-up questions — to reward models punishing any visible uncertainty, forcing the underlying probability distribution into miscalibration.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: Provides a generalizable diagnostic lens for evaluating any RLHF-tuned consumer chat product's reliability ceiling — useful when comparing chat-first labs (OpenAI, Anthropic) versus programmatic/API-first providers like TypeSafe.

insights.claim: TypeSafe deliberately avoids identity/persona fine-tuning (it will not train Jev to state it is 'Jev from TypeSafe') because baking in any such fixed fact 'fractures' the model's smooth, internet-consistent probability distribution and measurably degrades intelligence — a tradeoff Almeida says is acceptable for a first-party consumer product (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude) but wrong for an API model.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: Explains a specific technical reason API-model providers may resist brand/identity fine-tuning requests from customers, and offers a lens for evaluating claims that persona-tuning has hidden capability costs.

themes.theme: API Design — Structured Primitives Over Chat

insights.claim: Jev's three core output primitives are Nool (a calibrated continuous-probability boolean, named after 'Bernoulli'), Score (a continuous LM-judgment/ranking value), and Choice (a calibrated enum/switch, positioned as the correct replacement for OpenAI-style function calling) — deliberately built as new type-system concepts rather than reusing existing programming types like int, float, or bool.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: Defines the concrete API surface developers must learn to build on Jev; the deliberate avoidance of standard types signals TypeSafe is trying to establish a new programming primitive category, which raises both differentiation and adoption-friction considerations.
insights.quote: I think these map all to like programming primitives where like choice maps into like a like a switch statement on an enum. Um, nules map to if statements and scores map to sorting or thresholding at a greater than or less than.

insights.claim: All Jev inputs (state, instructions, criteria) are passed as structured JSON objects rather than templated into chat-style system-message strings; Almeida calls system messages 'disgusting global variables' that dump every instruction into one call instead of letting many small questions be asked and verified independently.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: A direct architectural rejection of the chat-prompt-template convention used by OpenAI/Anthropic-style APIs — investors should judge whether this structured-JSON approach becomes a genuine developer-experience moat or an adoption barrier versus familiar chat APIs.
insights.quote: System messages are like disgusting global variables where you just put everything in there and you put all the instructions at once.

insights.claim: Almeida's stated best practice for developers is to decompose tasks into many small, independently verifiable atomic questions (e.g., separate questions per refusal scenario) rather than one large system-prompt call, because he claims this personally benchmarked as faster, cheaper, and more accurate than a single monolithic call, and each atomic question can be measured, fixed, and turned into a permanent regression test.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: A concrete, actionable prompt-engineering/architecture pattern for teams building on Jev (or any LLM API) that claims measurable cost and quality gains over monolithic system-prompt pipelines.

insights.claim: Almeida recommends a specific cost-saving pattern: tag every item in a large shared state (e.g., messages in a conversation) with an ID once, then ask many independent, cheap, parallel questions against each ID — so the expensive state is 'paid for' once while extracting many answers from it.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: A directly actionable LLM-pipeline cost-optimization pattern developers can apply today, independent of which model provider they use.
insights.quote: put ids on every like message and then ask a question about each ID

insights.claim: Almeida says he personally fought against OpenAI's function-calling design because it lacks any confidence/probability signal per function choice, forcing developers to nudge tool selection today by 'begging' in system-message text (e.g., asking the model 'pretty please' to prefer a tool) — a problem he says still persists industry-wide with agent skills and MCP tool use.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, persistent gap in incumbent function-calling APIs (no native confidence weighting) that Jev's Choice primitive claims to solve — a concrete technical differentiator to validate against real developer tool-routing pain points.
insights.quote: I want to be removed from any project involving like function calling if you did not get a legit bias for each function.

insights.claim: Almeida claims existing coding-agent harnesses are 'highly overfit' to their own built-in toolset and use external tools/MCP integrations poorly because of that overfitting, with today's only lever to bias tool selection being informal system-message pleading rather than a structured signal.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: A specific, testable critique of current agent frameworks' tool-routing reliability that could inform how coding-agent vendors (or challengers) should prioritize architecture fixes.

insights.claim: TypeSafe self-identifies as fundamentally a 'data lab' rather than a pure model/architecture lab, arguing that model capability and reliability improvements ('nines') come overwhelmingly from data quality and shape rather than compute scale or architecture tweaks.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: Signals TypeSafe's hiring and R&D investment priority (it says it is 'hiring infinite data people') and suggests investors should evaluate the company's data-curation talent and pipeline as much as its model architecture claims.
insights.quote: to me model capabilities means data.

insights.claim: TypeSafe deliberately does not want to train on its own customers' API usage data, even though it believes it could obtain rights to do so, because real-world traffic follows a power law toward common/repeated queries that would overfit and 'fracture' the model away from the rare, futuristic use cases the company is targeting.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: A notable departure from the typical 'train on your API traffic' data flywheel strategy used by many LLM providers — relevant to how investors should model TypeSafe's long-term data moat versus competitors that do train on live usage.

insights.claim: Almeida offers a general scaling-law heuristic: a scaling law implies exponentially more resources are needed for typically sub-linear capability gains, which he calls 'a bad investment unless the linear gains are really really valuable' — implying compute-scaling bets should be judged case-by-case on the value of marginal gains, not treated as automatically worthwhile.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: A useful heuristic for investors evaluating capex-heavy frontier-scaling narratives: ask whether the marginal capability gain justifies the exponential resource cost for the specific use case, rather than assuming scale always pays off.

insights.claim: Echoing Sutton's 'Bitter Lesson,' Almeida argues that selecting the right training task/north star matters more than compute or raw data volume, noting that genuinely new post-training paradigms (RLHF, then RLVR) have emerged only about twice in LLM history — implying TypeSafe's claimed third paradigm (RLCD) would be a rare, defensible achievement if real.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: Frames paradigm-level training-task innovation as scarce and high-value; investors should weigh TypeSafe's RLCD claim as a potentially rare structural edge if it holds up to scrutiny, pending TypeSafe's promised future publication.

insights.claim: Almeida states that even given one billion dollars, he would not choose to pretrain a model from scratch, preferring cheaper composition/'Frankensteining' of existing capabilities via mid-training and targeted data work — and confirms TypeSafe is currently doing mid-training rather than full pretraining.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: Implies TypeSafe's cost structure and capital intensity is meaningfully lower than a full-pretraining frontier lab, which is directly relevant to its stated 'intelligence per dollar' economics and future fundraising/valuation framing.
insights.quote: if you gave me a billion dollars I wouldn't pre-train.

insights.claim: TypeSafe explicitly rejects strict determinism (identical input always producing identical output) as the wrong reliability target, instead optimizing for 'robustness' — similar inputs producing similar outputs — which it tests by inserting nonce/UUID tokens into semantically identical prompts and checking output consistency.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: Developers requiring strict reproducibility (e.g., for unit tests or audit trails) should note that Jev does not currently guarantee determinism by design choice, not just technical limitation — a due-diligence flag for regulated or compliance-sensitive use cases.
insights.quote: you want um given similar inputs get similar outputs.

insights.claim: Almeida concedes that despite his stated preference against determinism, customer/peer pressure (citing OpenAI's and Anthropic's own trajectories) could eventually force TypeSafe to offer deterministic or seeded model options regardless of his technical philosophy.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: Suggests determinism/seed support is a plausible future TypeSafe API feature investors and customers could reasonably expect, despite current messaging against it.

insights.claim: TypeSafe explicitly declines to promise indefinite stability of specific model versions/strings, saying it plans to iterate and ship new models faster than typical providers, and may eventually offer a formal long-term-support (LTS) tier once economics allow — but does not currently guarantee that today's Jev version will remain unchanged or continuously supported.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: A concrete operational risk for any team building production dependencies on the current Jev model version: version-pinning/breaking-change risk is real and acknowledged by the company itself, unlike vendors offering longer-term model-string guarantees.
insights.quote: we are not promising long-term support for the models

insights.claim: Almeida claims TypeSafe's platform already has more 'nines' of uptime than Anthropic despite having the least mature launch infrastructure among frontier providers, crediting an unusually strong internal platform engineering team.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: A specific competitive infrastructure-quality claim worth independently verifying via third-party uptime monitoring before weighting it into any reliability-based competitive comparison with Anthropic.
insights.quote: I think we have more up nines of uptime than anthropic while having the most unprecedented launch ever.

insights.claim: TypeSafe deliberately designs its platform so the company has no visibility into what downstream tasks or applications are being built on its API, arguing this decomposition-driven ignorance is intentional to maximize developer autonomy and avoid the platform becoming a moral/behavioral gatekeeper over use cases.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: A meaningfully different platform-governance posture than major labs that monitor/restrict API use cases — relevant to assessing TypeSafe's regulatory and reputational risk profile as it scales into more sensitive verticals.
insights.quote: It's none of my business, right?

insights.claim: Pre-launch validation of Jev was reportedly weak: more than half of test users did not understand the product, the company had almost no revenue before launch, and internal non-technical staff were fearful it wouldn't land — illustrating a 'vitamin, not painkiller' problem that only resolved once developers self-discovered concrete use cases post-launch.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: A cautionary data point that traditional pre-launch product validation (customer interviews, pilot revenue) may systematically undercount demand for genuinely novel developer-infrastructure categories — relevant when evaluating other pre-revenue infra startups against similar skepticism.
insights.quote: the most common thing was like I would say like more than half the people we had play with it just did not get it

insights.claim: TypeSafe maps its target use cases into four buckets: 'dark data' analysis (large enterprises with data previously too expensive to run through LLMs), coding agents, real-time/latency-sensitive intelligence (e.g., e-commerce, assistants), and 'smart software' that is intrinsically composable — with dark data and coding agents flagged as the largest expected revenue drivers by volume.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: Gives investors a concrete taxonomy for sizing which enterprise verticals (data-heavy incumbents, dev-tooling, latency-sensitive commerce) are most likely to become early large TypeSafe revenue segments.
insights.quote: this is like a data scientist's wet dream.

insights.claim: Almeida predicts today's dominant single-model coding agents (naming Claude Code and Codex as roughly the current #1 and #2) face a structural challenge because their architecture is built around one frontier chat/reasoning model, whereas open coding agents integrating Jev-style programmable models could find a killer differentiated use case that rapidly shifts market share.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: Flags a potential competitive disruption vector in the coding-agent market: multi-model/programmable-model integration versus incumbents locked into single-model architectures — worth monitoring for share shifts among coding-agent products.
insights.quote: cloud code and codeex are I believe the the winner like the the number one and two.

insights.claim: TypeSafe states a deliberate strategic bias toward serving individual developers/hackers ahead of enterprises, explicitly asking internally 'how can we launch things that are better for developers than enterprises,' a contrast to the standard SaaS PLG-to-enterprise-upsell funnel.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: Suggests TypeSafe's monetization path and loyalty-building strategy may deliberately lag typical enterprise-upsell economics in favor of developer goodwill — relevant to modeling near-term revenue mix versus long-term platform lock-in.

insights.claim: Almeida's central macro claim is that despite AI solving Millennium Prize-caliber math problems, it has automated roughly 0% (likely under 1%) of the world's economically valuable work so far, and this gap — not raw model capability — is the bottleneck TypeSafe is targeting; he predicts closing it will show up directly in GDP/productivity statistics rather than causing mass unemployment.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: Reframes the AI investment thesis away from 'more benchmark intelligence' toward 'automation integration bottleneck' — a lens for evaluating which AI companies are actually capturing the economic-automation opportunity versus just improving chat capability.
insights.quote: I think that all models are roughly tied right now at zero

insights.claim: Almeida references a stated goal tied to total factor productivity (TFP) growth reaching roughly 3% within five years as a macroeconomic outcome he wants AI-driven automation (and TypeSafe specifically) to help produce.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: A rare instance of an AI infrastructure founder tying company mission explicitly to a trackable macroeconomic growth metric (TFP), giving investors a long-horizon benchmark to monitor for whether the 'AI economic revolution' thesis materializes.

insights.claim: Almeida argues mainstream SaaS software in 2026 looks nearly identical to 2019 software plus 'a chat box on the side' because AI has not been trusted to make autonomous decisions with company stakes attached; he predicts this triggers an 'inverse SaaS apocalypse' in which incumbent SaaS vendors — who best understand which decisions are worth automating — get supercharged by machine-native AI rather than disrupted by it.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: A contrarian call against the common 'AI kills SaaS' narrative — implies investors should look for incumbent SaaS players integrating machine-native/programmable AI as beneficiaries rather than assuming AI-native startups will primarily displace them.
insights.quote: I think it's going to be like an inverse SAS apocalypse. I think SAS is going to be supercharged by this.

insights.claim: Almeida recounts personally pushing to ship InstructGPT at OpenAI using an unpublished internal PPO-based algorithm he built himself; it reportedly captured roughly 50% of contemporaneous LLM market share immediately, but its dominant real-world use collapsed into AI-generated marketing copy ('slop'), which he says directly shaped his belief that intelligence must be consumed by code/software rather than chat to create durable economic value.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: An insider account of how a hit chat product (InstructGPT) can still fail to translate into durable economic value if consumption stays human-chat-centric — the origin story directly underpinning TypeSafe's code-as-consumer thesis.
insights.quote: basically immediately it took 50% of the market share of LLMs at the time

insights.claim: Almeida says that when he pitched his 'code-consumed intelligence' thesis to Sam Altman while still at OpenAI, Altman encouraged him to pursue it, but OpenAI's internal instruction-following team believed the problem was already 'solved,' implying OpenAI passed on or deprioritized the exact machine-native automation thesis TypeSafe later built its company around.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: Suggests a specific strategic blind spot at OpenAI (treating instruction-following as 'solved') that created the opening TypeSafe exploited — relevant context for evaluating whether other frontier labs have similar unaddressed gaps competitors could exploit.
insights.quote: Sam was like this is so good. You should go work on it.

insights.claim: Almeida is broadly dismissive of the current wave of new foundation-model startups ('neolabs'), calling most of them 'crap' that destroy rather than create value by redoing frontier work from scratch with low odds of moving the frontier, and arguing that investors/founders overvaluing 'pure research pedigree' over task-focused conviction is backwards.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: A pointed, founder-level critique directly relevant to VC diligence on new AI-lab startups: Almeida argues research pedigree and generic scaling ambition are weak signals, while a clearly differentiated task/north-star is the signal that matters.
insights.quote: I think most Neolabs are crap.

themes.theme: Future R&D — Coding Agents & the KV-Cache Bottleneck

insights.claim: Almeida argues current coding agents are architecturally constrained by what he calls 'the tyranny of the KV cache': because efficient inference requires continuously appending to one growing context, agents get locked into a single model and discouraged from good state-management, abstraction, and decomposition practices — which he says explains why routing is hard, sub-agents underperform, and context compaction remains an unsolved problem.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: Offers a concrete technical explanation for several widely-observed coding-agent limitations (poor sub-agent performance, brittle context compaction) that could inform where the next generation of coding-agent architecture innovation happens.
insights.quote: coding agents free from the tyranny of the KV cache

insights.claim: Almeida is drafting (subject to internal team veto) an unpublished document proposing coding-agent redesigns: labeled/hierarchical subtask trees that can be searched for relevant context on demand, sub-agents sharing state directly through shared memory rather than passing full context back to a parent process, and using cheaper intelligence specifically to manage and route state between agents.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: A potential future TypeSafe research publication or product direction (agent state-management/routing) worth watching, as it could reshape coding-agent architecture beyond the current single-context-window paradigm.

insights.claim: Voice-controlled computer-use agents built on Jev emerged organically from developer experimentation rather than being an initial TypeSafe design target, and Almeida says the company believes it can meaningfully improve the underlying model specifically for this use case going forward.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: Flags computer-use/voice-agent control as an emergent, unplanned Jev application vertical that TypeSafe intends to invest in further — a category investors should watch for dedicated TypeSafe product announcements.

insights.claim: Almeida frames TypeSafe's long-term ambition as becoming an 'AWS of intelligence' — a horizontal platform offering many differentiated 'shapes' of machine-native intelligence rather than a single model — comparing today's Jev to 'TCP' with, in his words, 'seven more layers to go' in the stack still to be built.
insights.speaker: Diogo Almeida
insights.so_what: Signals TypeSafe's self-conception as an infrastructure-layer platform play analogous to cloud computing's evolution, relevant to long-term valuation framing (platform vs. single-product company).
insights.quote: there's going to be like an AWS of like intelligence, you know
